chunks: And as for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Baraqi from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who sells a slave girl whom he has been abstaining from (sexual relations) with, is there upon him [the requirement of] istibra' (waiting period for pregnancy verification) from her? He said: Yes. And [I asked] about the minimum that suffices for istibra' for the buyer and the sold girl. He said: The people of Medina say: one menstruation. And Ja'far (peace be upon him) says: two menstruations. And I asked him about the minimum istibra' of a virgin. He said: The people of Medina say: one menstruation. And Ja'far (peace be upon him) used to say: two menstruations. So the way to handle this hadith is to carry it upon a type of recommendation (istihbab). And he clarified that in the preceding hadith by his saying: If he verifies her pregnancy with another menstruation, there is no harm; it is in the position of excess.

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْمَدِينَة: People of Medina: Referring to the jurists of Medina, often cited in hadith for their legal opinions.
key_terms.اسْتِبْرَاء: Istibra: The waiting period for a female slave to verify she is not pregnant before being sold or married off.
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَاب: Recommendation: A legal status where an action is rewarded but not obligatory, and omitting it is not penalized.
key_terms.الْبِكْر: Virgin: A female who has not yet menstruated or is young, requiring a different ruling for istibra.
key_terms.جَارِيَة: Slave girl: A female slave, specifically in the context of pre-modern Islamic law.
key_terms.حَيْضَة: Menstruation: Used here as the unit of time for the waiting period.

ai.seo_question: What is the required waiting period (istibra) for a purchased slave girl according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's chain in *al-Istibsar* addresses the fiqh of 'istibra' for a purchased slave girl, contrasting the Medinan practice of one menstruation with Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq’s (AS) preference for two. The scholar clarifies that the Imam’s stricter view is not a binding obligation but a recommended precaution (istihbab), thereby harmonizing the two positions and allowing flexibility in legal practice. This reflects the Shia methodology of distinguishing between obligatory certainty and recommended caution in matters of personal status.
